article.overview: A Doppler lidar is a laser instrument that measures how fast a vehicle is moving and how far it is above the ground, using the shift in frequency of light reflected from the surface. The best-documented example is NASA Langley Research Center's Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL), a coherent, frequency-modulated sensor designed to give landing vehicles velocity and altitude data during descent [1][2]. NDL was tested in closed-loop flights on the Morpheus rocket-propelled lander, as described in a 2015 AIAA paper [4]. It also flew on Intuitive Machines' Odysseus (IM-1) lunar lander, which landed in the lunar South Pole region in February 2024 [6]. It is a landing-navigation sensor rather than a surface science instrument.
article.description:
A Doppler lidar combines two measurements. The first is range: how far the laser light travels to the ground and back. The second is the Doppler shift: the change in the light's frequency caused by motion along the beam. Together they give the speed and height of a moving vehicle relative to the surface. For a landing sensor, the important quantities are the vehicle's velocity components and its height above the ground [1][2].

NDL was developed at NASA Langley to provide these measurements in a compact package as an alternative to radar. NASA describes the instrument as operating at a frequency three to four orders of magnitude higher than radar, which it says enables much higher precision velocity and altitude measurements. NASA also states that it is at least 50 percent smaller in mass, size and required power than typical current radars [5].

The catalogue entry is generic. This article uses NDL as the principal documented example because it is the Doppler lidar with the most published information in the sources reviewed. Other Doppler lidar designs are not covered here.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
- Descent velocity and altitude measurement. The main purpose is to give a lander's guidance and navigation system velocity and altitude information during the final part of descent. The release describes this as useful over bodies such as the Moon or Mars, where GPS is unavailable [2].
- Hazard-relative landing. In the ALHAT-based Morpheus tests, the Doppler lidar supplied velocity and range measurements to the navigation filter that guided the lander to a site chosen from a hazard field with rocks, craters and slopes [4].
- Trajectory reconstruction and data products. The 2025 AIAA paper describes how NDL data support trajectory reconstruction and animation for IM-1, and discusses possible future uses of the mission data [1].
- Technology demonstration for future landers. The IM-1 flight was presented as a demonstration of a small, lower-cost, lower-risk landing sensor that could be an alternative to radar on future missions [2].
article.operating_principle:
A Doppler lidar transmits laser light toward the ground and analyses the light that returns. NDL is a coherent, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) system. The laser frequency is varied in a known pattern, so the instrument can compare returned light with transmitted light to determine range. Motion along the beam shifts the returned frequency, which gives the line-of-sight velocity [1][2].

NDL transmits three laser beams at fixed, different angles and measures range and velocity along each one. Combining the three line-of-sight measurements gives the vehicle's three velocity components and its altitude [2]. The published sources do not give the laser wavelength or the beam geometry in full detail, so the exact optical design cannot be reconstructed from them.
article.scientific_importance:
Safe landing depends on accurate knowledge of a vehicle's velocity and height in the final stage of descent. Radar sensors have been used for this purpose for decades. NDL was developed to offer higher precision in a smaller package [1][5]. Its test flights provide the main evidence that a coherent Doppler lidar can work in the landing environment. The Morpheus closed-loop tests reported that the sensor met its expected accuracy levels [4], and the IM-1 flight was presented as a demonstration of the same sensor on a commercial lunar lander [1][2].

Its scientific importance is mainly technological. It is a navigation sensor that could support more precise landings on future missions. Each new mission would need its own verification of performance, because the reported results come from a small number of tests and one lunar flight.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a Doppler lidar. The sources reviewed describe NDL in several configurations: engineering test units used in ground and flight tests, and the flight configuration used on IM-1. Published mass, size, power and wavelength figures for the flight configuration were not found in the primary sources read. A mass figure in a conference slide summary was not verified against the original document and is therefore not reported.

examples.name: NASA Navigation Doppler Lidar (NDL) on Intuitive Machines IM-1 (Odysseus)
examples.type: Flown lunar lander navigation sensor (IM-1 mission, February 2024)
examples.beam_description: Three laser beams at fixed, different angles.

reported_flight_performance.basis: Press release (Optica, 3 October 2024) and accompanying conference presentation. The 2025 AIAA paper abstract describes the performance as exceptional but gives no numbers.

examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
examples.laser_wavelength: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
examples.role_during_landing: NASA reports that NDL collected data during powered descent and landing. The company later stated that NDL did not assist the landing because a technical issue stopped NDL from sending data to Odysseus. NASA's project scientist said all NDL data were received and that the instrument worked far better than they expected. The accounts are not reconciled in the sources read.

examples.name: NDL engineering test units in Morpheus flights and Langley runway tests
examples.type: Engineering test unit (ETU) built to mimic flight hardware, used in closed-loop flight tests on Morpheus and in ground tests at NASA Langley. The test dates for the runway test are not stated in the source read.
examples.stated_precision_2022_paper: Operation from over five kilometres altitude, with velocity and range precision of within a few cm/sec and a few meters precision, respectively, depending on the vehicle dynamics.
examples.ground_test: Telescopes set up about a quarter-mile outside a 1.9-mile runway, with a target in the back of a truck moving at 5 to 10 mph. NASA states the test covered 2.4 miles and that the projected maximum lunar range is about five miles after subtracting atmospheric effects.
examples.known_limitation: Susceptible to signal degradation due to air heated by the rocket engine (2015 abstract).
examples.dimensions: A small electronics box connected by fibre-optic cables to three telescopes. No absolute dimensions verified.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources read.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: NASA describes the instrument as a small electronics box connected by fibre-optic cables to three telescopes. No absolute dimensions, mass or power value for the flight configuration was verified from a primary source. NASA's statement that the instrument is at least 50 percent smaller in mass, size and required power than typical current radars is a relative comparison only.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No verified mass value for the flight configuration. The mass figure found in a conference slide summary was not verified against the original document and is not reported.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A Doppler lidar must measure through the thermal and optical conditions created during descent. The 2015 abstract identifies signal degradation from heated air as a limitation [4]. The 2024 release attributes the better-than-projected IM-1 results partly to lower vehicle vibration and higher surface reflectivity than assumed in conservative estimates [2]. Measurement quality therefore depends on the vehicle's motion and on the reflectivity of the surface being observed.

Thermal, vacuum and radiation qualification levels for the flight unit are not publicly specified in the sources read. The article does not assume any environmental tolerance that the sources do not state.
article.limitations:
The sources reviewed do not publish mass, power or cost figures for the flight configuration. NASA's comparisons with radar are relative [5]. The reported precision depends on vehicle dynamics [3] and on the test setup, so the figures from the 2015, 2022 and 2024 sources should not be combined into a single specification. The heated-air effect identified in 2015 [4] has not been characterised for the IM-1 flight in the sources read.

The only lunar flight evidence reviewed is a single demonstration on IM-1. The 2024 release attributes part of the result to lower vibration and higher surface reflectivity than assumed [2], and the sources read do not assess performance in less favourable conditions. The two accounts of NDL's role during IM-1 landing are not reconciled in the sources [6][7].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A Doppler lidar is a descent sensor, not a surface payload. Its deployment means mounting it on the descending vehicle so that its beams view the surface along the descent path.
transportation_process: Earth integration and launch: the lander's own laser altimeter had not been activated before launch. In the hours before landing, the navigation software was patched to use NDL data instead [7].
Lunar transfer and landing: the IM-1 lander descended and touched down in the lunar South Pole region on 22 February 2024 [6].

Deployment methods: NDL was carried as a NASA payload on a commercial lander under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme [6]. The electronics box is connected to the three telescopes by fibre-optic cables [5], which suggests separate optical heads and electronics. Mounting positions, fields of view and interfaces for IM-1 were not verified in the sources read.
Historical examples: in the Morpheus closed-loop tests, the Doppler lidar supplied velocity and range measurements to the ALHAT navigation filter during descent from 250 m [4].

The electronics box is connected to the three telescopes by fibre-optic cables [5], which suggests separate optical heads and electronics. Mounting positions, fields of view and interfaces for IM-1 were not verified in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: In the Morpheus closed-loop tests, the Doppler lidar supplied velocity and range measurements to the ALHAT navigation filter during descent from 250 m [4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The only flight evidence is on Odysseus. Compatibility with any other lander would need verified mounting, field-of-view, power, data and vibration interfaces, which are not available in the sources reviewed. The article does not assert compatibility with any named lander.

article.historical_significance: The Morpheus tests were described as the culmination of the TRL 6 work for the lidar suite of the ALHAT project [4]. The IM-1 flight is the first reported use of NDL on a lunar landing in the sources reviewed [1][2]. NASA described the mission as the first time in more than 50 years that an American organization had landed instruments on the Moon [6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
The term Doppler lidar describes a measurement method rather than one standard instrument. The NDL figures in this article come from several sources that test different things. The 2015 abstract reports velocity accuracy of 0.2 cm/s and range accuracy of 17 cm [4]. The 2022 paper reports precision of a few cm/s and a few metres depending on vehicle dynamics [3]. The 2024 release reports precision better than 0.8 cm/s and 0.8 m for IM-1 [2]. These values should be treated as results for specific tests, not as a single specification.

Evidence gaps:
- Mass, dimensions, power, laser wavelength and beam geometry for the flight configuration are not publicly specified in the sources read.
- The full IM-1 technical paper with trajectory reconstruction (Karlgaard et al., NASA NTRS record 20250008015) was identified but not read in full, so its detailed results are not reported here.
- The role of NDL data during IM-1 landing is disputed between NASA's account [6] and the company's account [7].
- The number of Morpheus flights and the details of any dust-related data dropouts were not confirmed in the 2015 abstract [4]. The abstract reports signal degradation from heated air but no Doppler-lidar dropout figures.
- Other reported NDL details, such as a 2021 suborbital test flight and a specific range-rate limit, were found only in secondary summaries and are not included.
- No independent assessment of the IM-1 flight data was found in the sources read.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed (none were present). Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Mass, dimensions, power and laser wavelength for the NDL flight configuration are not publicly specified in the sources read. A mass figure (15 kg engineering test unit) seen only in a conference slide summary was not verified and is not reported.
NASA and the company give different accounts of whether NDL data assisted the IM-1 landing. Both are reported; neither is resolved.
The Karlgaard et al. IM-1 trajectory reconstruction paper (NTRS record 20250008015) was identified but its PDF could not be read, so its detailed results are not included.
Performance figures come from different tests (2015 Morpheus abstract, 2022 conference paper, 2024 press release and presentation) and are not directly comparable.

Claims from search-result summaries that could not be verified against a primary source (a 2021 New Shepard flight, a 20 cm/s landing-vehicle velocity error, a 20 Hz data rate, and a 120 degree beam separation) are omitted.

Morpheus Doppler-lidar data dropouts from engine dust were suggested in a secondary summary but are not reported by the 2015 abstract, which cites signal degradation from heated air instead; the full paper was not read.

Image URLs were checked for an image/jpeg response; the full-resolution download and rights status were not separately checked. Both images are ground-test photographs of the engineering test unit, not lunar operation.
